talks.title: Continuous Integration / Continuous Disaster by 0x57696c6c
talks.teaser: Reviews continuous Integration / Continuous Disaster by 0x57696c6c and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
CI/CD Foundations and Risk

Will Alexander, a Palo Alto Networks red teamer, introduces CI/CD as automated build, test, and delivery through ephemeral runners. He contrasts marketed security benefits with real supply-chain failures such as SolarWinds Orion backdooring, compromised npm packages, and trojanized CCleaner builds.

Attack Scenarios

Three assumed-breach exercises cover a poisoned Debian dependency in a GitLab pipeline, malicious VS Code extensions, and multi-pipeline compromise. In the first, a backdoored package on a Kubernetes runner establishes C2; hung jobs may alert developers because builds normally finish quickly.

Abusing Pipeline Tokens

CI job tokens authenticate to GitLab APIs with the pipeline owner’s permissions across all accessible repositories—not just the active project. While jobs run, attackers exfiltrated 400+ projects (~4.5 GB) using a tool called GitLabrador Retriever, illustrating over-permissive developer accounts.

Defensive Takeaways

Alexander closes with DevSecOps mitigations Palo Alto implements and broader supply-chain controls, framing CI/CD as high-impact terrain when humans introduce secrets, third-party code, or misconfigurations.

talks.title: Vulnerability Management for Containers by Scott Wilson
talks.teaser: Examines vulnerability Management for Containers by Scott Wilson and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Talk Scope and Goals

Scott Wilson of IBM X-Force Red frames container vulnerability management for CarolinaCon Online. He distinguishes scanning from broader container hardening, orchestration deep dives, and vendor sales pitches.

Containers vs VMs and the 4Cs

Containers are portable, layered runtimes sharing a host OS, unlike VMs that duplicate full guest operating systems. He walks through images, runtime engines like Docker, and the cloud-cluster-container-code security model that expands attack surface when poorly managed.

CI/CD, Scanning, and Tooling

The talk covers how container adoption changes vulnerability management versus twenty years of host scanning. Wilson outlines development pipeline risks, scanning strategies, marketplace tool tradeoffs, Kubernetes admission controllers, and compliance considerations for container fleets.

Takeaways

Attendees should leave able to discuss how to scan, prioritize, and govern container vulnerabilities with development and security teams.

talks.title: Tales from the Usenet by Jason Evans
talks.teaser: Demonstrates tales from the Usenet by Jason Evans and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
What is Usenet

SUSE training engineer and Big Eight board member Jason Evans describes Usenet as a decentralized peer-to-peer newsgroup system predating the modern internet—messages called articles exchanged among news servers with no central authority, maintained largely by volunteers.

Origins and growth

In 1979–1980 Duke and UNC students used Unix uucp and PDP-11s to build multi-machine discussion beyond single-host email. Presentations at Usenix sparked explosive growth to hundreds of nodes by 1981, expanding globally by 1993 as landlines replaced costly modem hops.

Golden age and decline

Universities inculturated newcomers each September until AOL offered Usenet in 1993 without that mentorship—eternal September—flooding communities with untrained users. Evans shares Gene Spafford's famous metaphor of Usenet as performing elephants with diarrhea: inspiring, unwieldy, and prolific—reflecting its chaotic golden age around 1992.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Jason Evans, a training engineer for SUSE Linux, Tor Project volunteer, and board member of the Usenet Big-8 Management Board, delivers a historical and technical overview of Usenet's architecture, cultural impact, and governance. Tracing Usenet from its 1979 inception between Duke University and UNC across dial-up modems through its 1990s golden age, ISP decommissioning, and modern revival, Evans explores the technical strengths and vulnerabilities of decentralized store-and-forward protocols. The presentation details seminal moments in computer security and open-source history hosted on Usenet, including the origin of Linux, the Kremvax spoof, early Cypherpunk cryptography discussions, and Phil Zimmermann's release of PGP.

Key Topics:
- Architecture of Usenet: peer-to-peer, store-and-forward news synchronization via UUCP and NNTP
- Evolution and decline: dial-up constraints, "Eternal September," binary newsgroup abuse, ISP drop-off, and Google Groups spam
- Usenet governance: the collapse and 2020 resurrection of the Big-8 Management Board (chartering comp.infosystems.gemini)
- Seminal milestones in hacker history: the 1984 Kremvax spoof, Linus Torvalds' Linux announcement, Cypherpunks (alt.cypherpunks), and Phil Zimmermann's PGP distribution

Technical Details:
Conceived in November 1979 by graduate students at Duke University and the University of North Carolina, Usenet was created on PDP-11 minicomputers running Unix Version 7 to exchange long-form threaded articles. Initially operating without the ARPANET or a centralized backbone, the network leveraged uucp (Unix-to-Unix Copy) over 300-baud dial-up modems. Messages ("articles") propagated asynchronously in a store-and-forward peer-to-peer topology where each news server synchronized local article spools with downstream peers. By the early 1990s, the system transitioned to the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) over TCP/IP, expanding into a worldwide network spanning corporate, university, and international research nodes across Europe, Australia, and the post-Soviet Eastern bloc.

Because Usenet was architected on mutual trust among academic operators, it lacked native sender authentication, central moderation, or cryptographic integrity verification. This structural absence of access control manifested in early security incidents, such as the April 1, 1984 "Kremvax" hoax, where an attacker easily spoofed article headers to masquerade as the Soviet Union’s first Usenet site. In the 1990s and 2000s, commercial ISPs faced mounting abuse, particularly from massive binary newsgroups (alt.binaries.*) distributing unauthorized content, while Google Groups integrated Deja News without robust spam mitigations, flooding newsgroups with unthrottled spam. Consequently, between 2005 and 2009, major providers (AOL, Verizon, Sprint, Time Warner, and Duke University) shut down their NNTP servers.

Evans discusses revitalizing the network’s administrative backbone. In 2014, the Usenet Big-8 Management Board—responsible for governing traditional hierarchies (comp.*, sci.*, talk.*, etc.)—became inactive, preventing newsgroup additions or deletions. In 2020, Evans, Tristan Miller, and a third colleague formally reconstituted the board, re-establishing group management workflows and chartering new groups such as comp.infosystems.gemini. The talk highlights Usenet’s historic role in distributed collaboration, citing Linus Torvalds’ August 1991 Linux announcement on comp.os.minix, the seminal Tanenbaum-Torvalds microkernel debate, Tim May’s digital cash essays on alt.cypherpunks, Colin Needham's distribution of IMDb shell scripts on rec.arts.movies, and Phil Zimmermann posting PGP 1.0 source code in 1991 to circumvent federal munitions export controls.

Key Takeaways:
Usenet established the technical and philosophical blueprint for decentralized, censorship-resistant communication protocols long before the modern web. However, its historical trajectory demonstrates that open, peer-to-peer messaging networks cannot survive long-term without effective, protocol-level abuse defenses and spam countermeasures, as relying solely on client-side killfiles shifts an unsustainable burden onto users. Community-driven governance models, exemplified by the Big-8 Management Board, remain vital for preserving public protocol standards independent of centralized commercial platforms.

talks.title: Security is an Awesome Product Feature by Mark Hahn
talks.teaser: Details security is an Awesome Product Feature by Mark Hahn and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Security From a Builder's Perspective

Mark Hahn, director of cloud strategy, SRE, and DevOps with 30 years shipping trading, supply-chain, and payment software, argues security must be a product feature—not a gate at the end of development. His lens is application-centric: reliable software that doesn't page operators at 3 a.m.

## Empowering Development Teams

Product engineers need tools, permissions, and CI/CD pipelines to move from idea to monitored production quickly. Security woven into that flow beats bolt-on reviews that slow creativity without improving outcomes.

## Requirements That Stick

Hahn maps regulatory mandates (PCI, HIPAA, financial data rules) to concrete engineering practices—modern TLS, current cipher suites, and contractual obligations customers already expect. Browsers phasing out weak crypto shows how platform shifts enforce baseline hygiene.

## Making Security Sellable

When security enables trust, uptime, and compliance, it becomes a competitive advantage customers understand. Hahn urges leaders to fund secure delivery the same way they fund features, because trustworthy products are simply better products.
